abstract: Maternal protein restriction is a well-established model of developmental programming, yet its consequences for behavior and cognition across the second half of life, and how these differ between sexes, remain poorly characterized. We fed C57BL/6J dams a normal-protein (NP, 17%) or low-protein (LP, 6%) diet throughout gestation and followed male and female offspring with an integrated battery assessing reward sensitivity, locomotion, anxiety-like behavior, social behavior, recognition memory, spatial learning and cognitive flexibility at 12 (middle age) and 18 months (old age). Maternal care was quantified from postnatal days 2 to 9. LP offspring of both sexes were born lighter and caught up by postnatal day 7. LP dams spent more time self-grooming, with longer self-grooming bouts, and took longer to retrieve their pups, whereas licking/grooming, its fragmentation and nursing were unchanged. Middle-aged LP males showed anhedonia-like behavior, anxiety-like behavior in the elevated plus-maze, reduced exploration and impaired short-term object recognition; in old age, affective indices normalized, but males became hyperactive and used less efficient search strategies in the Barnes maze. Middle-aged LP females showed hyperactivity, stereotypy and thigmotaxis; at 18 months they developed anhedonia-like behavior yet retained long-term object, social and spatial memory that had declined in aged NP females. A qualitative comparison with a prenatal-stress cohort tested in the same laboratory with the same battery revealed an overlapping, sex- and age-specific signature, particularly for the timing of anhedonia and for late-life memory outcomes. Gestational protein restriction, therefore, programs domain-specific and sexually divergent behavioral aging trajectories rather than uniform cognitive decline. These findings support sex-stratified, life-course designs in fetal programming research.
